items.title: Optimizing Agentic Artificial Intelligence to Improve Business Process Automation Efficiency through Modern Digital Technology
items.abstract: In the era of digital transformation, traditional Business Process Automation (BPA) still faces limitations in handling dynamic, unstructured, and complex decision-making tasks. Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI), which is characterized by autonomous agents capable of advanced reasoning, dynamic planning, and multi-step workflow execution, is considered a promising approach to improving the efficiency and adaptability of enterprise operations. This study aims to examine how Agentic AI can be optimized to improve BPA performance within modern digital ecosystems. Using a qualitative approach through a literature study, this paper synthesizes recent academic literature, theoretical models, and technological frameworks related to intelligent automation. The review indicates that integrating Agentic AI into enterprise business architectures has the potential to move beyond rigid, rule-based automation by enabling adaptive problem-solving, real-time context awareness, and cross-system collaboration. The reviewed literature also suggests that autonomous agents may help reduce operational bottlenecks, lower human intervention in routine cognitive workflows, and support more efficient resource allocation across organizational functions. In addition, this study identifies key implementation challenges, including system interoperability, algorithmic transparency, data privacy risks, and the governance mechanisms required for secure deployment. This study contributes to the literature on enterprise automation by proposing strategic considerations for organizations that seek to use digital technology to build more resilient, scalable, and intelligent business processes. Because this is a literature-based study, the findings are conceptual and do not provide empirical evidence of efficiency gains.

items.title: PERSISTENT HOMOLOGY ON LOCAL EXPLANATION SPACES: A TOPOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK FOR EXPLAINABLE AI IN DECISION SUPPORT SYSTEMS
items.abstract: We propose a novel framework that re-architects explainable artificial intelligence within decision support systems by integrating persistent homology into the explanation pipeline. Conventional approaches treat local feature attributions, such as SHAP values, as isolated scalar values for individual predictions, thereby overlooking the multi-scale interaction structures that emerge across a dataset. To address this limitation, we embed a collection of local explanation vectors into a metric space and compute persistent homology using the Vietoris-Rips complex. This topological analysis yields a set of persistence diagrams that capture the birth and death of homology generators across multiple scales. From these diagrams, we construct a global interaction tensor that encodes the total persistence of topological features involving pairs of input features. This tensor is then incorporated into the decision support system’s utility model as a regularization term, which penalizes or rewards the co-occurrence of high-magnitude attributions on features that persistently interact across the dataset. The resulting system provides decision-makers with queryable, multi-scale explanations at selectable persistence thresholds, transforming the interface from a static explainer into a dynamic topological reasoning tool. For instance, a user can request all feature pairs with persistence above a given threshold in a specific homology dimension, and the system highlights those interactions in the explanation. The proposed method is realized using the Ripser algorithm for efficient computation on datasets of up to one hundred thousand instances, with periodic updates via a streaming variant. Our contribution is a principled mathematical framework that bridges topological data analysis and explainable AI, offering a new perspective on feature interaction discovery and explanation stability. The significance lies in its ability to reveal robust, higher-order interaction structures that are invisible to standard attribution methods, thereby enhancing the interpretability and trustworthiness of model-driven decisions.

items.title: Preserving Human Judgment in AI-Enabled Education: The SAM Model for AI Readiness, Assessment, and Human-in-the-Loop Decision Making
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) shifts educational focus from access to information toward judging machine-generated claims and regulating the division of epistemic work. This conceptual article proposes the SAM model—self-regulation (S), ambiguity tolerance (A), and methodological competence (M)—as a bounded person-level resource model within broader AI readiness, with educators’ AI readiness as a central application. S denotes regulatory capacity, A a disposition-like willingness to tolerate unresolved epistemic ambiguity, and M the capacity to evaluate claims, differentiated into cross-domain M1 and domain-specific M2. SAM’s distinctive claim is configurational: M should predict independently assessed judgment more strongly at higher S and, under high ambiguity, when A is higher. These relations, the M1/M2 distinction, limited compensability, and incremental prediction beyond shared and neighboring accounts remain hypothetical. The model separates resources from enacted processes, contextual affordances, and outcomes and requires independent performance criteria. For AI-based assessment and learning analytics, educators’ interpretations of AI-derived evidence and construct inferences from behavioral traces require validated mappings addressing alternative explanations, comparability, fairness, and use. SAM thus offers a research agenda predicting when AI support preserves human judgment rather than merely improving supported performance.

items.title: Prevalence and correlates of GenerativeAI chatbot use for mental health concerns in higher education students
items.abstract: Background Large language model chatbots are increasingly used for mental health help-seeking, with general-purpose systems like ChatGPT becoming popular among young adults despite concerns about accuracy and misinformation. High rates of mental distress in higher education attending emerging adults make them an important focal population to characterize and contextual the use of generativeAI models for mental health in. Methods Data were collected from the 2024-2025 Healthy Minds Study at a large, public 4-year university. Of 12,000 students invited, 2071 participated; 896 bachelor-level students aged 18–24 years were randomly selected to complete a module with generativeAI questions, and 809 (90.2%) had complete data. Measures included chatbot use for mental health support, perceived AI trustworthiness, AI knowledge, mental health diagnosis, perceived need for help, past-year mental health treatment, barriers to care, other forms of informal help-seeking, and demographics. Weighted logistic regression models examined associations between these variables and chatbot use for mental health support. Results 15.4% of students reported using generalized chatbots for mental health help-seeking. Significant correlates included greater perceived need for help, experiencing more barriers to clinical care use, higher perceived trust in AI for mental health information, lower AI knowledge, and identifying as Asian. Specific barriers of financial constraints, limited time, fear of clinician mistreatment due to identity and privacy concerns were linked to chatbot usage. Conclusions GenerativeAI chatbots are a notable source of mental health support for college students, especially among those facing access barriers and who perceive AI as trustworthy. Future initiatives should educate young adults about chatbot capabilities and limitations and promote equitable mental health support.

items.title: Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative AI : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes
items.abstract: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT. Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity. Implications for practice and/or policy Prompt engineering can be used to simulate emotional support and personalize guidance based on SRL and emotion regulation principles, providing design considerations for future learner‐centred GenAI systems. Developers and educators aiming to design pedagogically meaningful GenAI tools should focus on scaffolding SRL both cognitively and emotionally, to support the affective and self‐regulatory dimensions of learning. We make the technical specifications and system prompts publicly available.

items.title: Psychological correlates of dependence on generative and conversational AI: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background. Dependence on generative and conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is measured with diverse instruments spanning addiction criteria, task reliance, and emotional bonding. No meta-analysis has pooled its psychological correlates across populations. Methods. We conducted a pre-registered three-level meta-analysis (Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.23420672) searching eight electronic databases and citations of instrument papers on 16 October 2026, with citation chasing. Zero-order correlations were pooled using correlated and hierarchical effects models on Fisher's z with cluster-robust inference (CR2). Scale type (T1 addiction-type, T2 functional, T3 emotional, T4 mixed) was the primary moderator. Certainty was rated via GRADE. Results. We included 127 samples (123 studies; N = 74,492; 29 countries; 70% university students; 39% mainland China). AI dependence correlated moderately with anxiety (r = 0.37, 95% CI [0.25, 0.48]), stress (r = 0.35 [0.25, 0.43]), depression (r = 0.32 [0.21, 0.42]), social anxiety (r = 0.36 [0.17, 0.53]), loneliness (r = 0.28 [0.18, 0.38]), and procrastination (r = 0.26 [0.12, 0.40]), and weakly and inversely with self-esteem (r = −0.18 [−0.35, −0.00]). All 95% prediction intervals crossed zero. Addiction-type and mixed scales showed no detectable difference; functional and emotional scales were rarely paired with clinical outcomes. Certainty was low to very low. Conclusions. AI dependence moderately correlates with distress and self-regulation difficulties, but prediction intervals cross zero and evidence certainty is low. Functional and emotional dependence have rarely been studied alongside clinical outcomes.

items.title: Registered Nurses' Experiences of Clinical Decision‐Making: A Qualitative Descriptive Study to Inform Artificial Intelligence‐Assisted Decision Support in Nursing
items.abstract: AIM: To describe registered nurses' experiences of clinical decision-making and identify needs that may inform future development of artificial-intelligence-assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. DESIGN: A qualitative descriptive study. METHODS: Data were collected between 2022 and 2025 through 16 semi-structured interviews with registered nurses working in inpatient wards at a Finnish university hospital. The data were analysed using inductive content analysis. RESULTS: Perceived challenges in clinical decision-making were related to organisational issues, multiprofessional collaboration, nurse-patient interactions, professional factors and availability and trustworthiness of data. The findings also identified support needs related to health information management, clinical workflows and quality of nursing care that may inform future artificial intelligence-assisted clinical decision support system development. CONCLUSION: Nurses experienced multifaceted challenges and needs in clinical decision-making, shaped by organisational, professional, relational and information-related factors. Adoption of artificial intelligence-assisted decision support systems may represent one potential approach to optimising clinical decision-making, improving patient care quality and enhancing workflow efficiency. Realising these opportunities requires coordinated efforts at individual, organisational and societal levels, including competence development, workflow redesign, strong data governance and a culture that fosters trust in technology. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE: The findings may inform the future development of artificial intelligence-assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. REPORTING METHOD: The Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research checklist was used when reporting the results. This paper addresses existing gaps and unmet needs in nursing clinical decision-making What were the main findings? The main findings highlight several key opportunities for artificial intelligence-assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. Where and on whom will the research have an impact? The research may inform efforts to optimise health information management, streamline clinical workflows and improve the quality of nursing care.

items.abstract: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Modern Banking Services: Benefits, Customer Experience and Challenges This research investigates the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in modern banking services, with particular emphasis on operational efficiency, customer experience, and emerging challenges. It examines the application of AI-driven technologies, including machine learning, intelligent chatbots, predictive analytics, and automated fraud detection, in streamlining banking operations, enhancing service personalisation, improving risk management, and supporting data-driven decision-making. Furthermore, the study evaluates key concerns associated with AI adoption, including data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, transparency, and customer trust. By assessing both the benefits and limitations of AI integration, this research aims to develop a comprehensive understanding of its implications for the banking sector and highlight the importance of responsible, secure, and customer-centric AI implementation in the evolving financial services landscape.

items.title: Savoir / Action — English Translation (V1)
items.abstract: An AI agent can be given an objective by a human, then search, interpret, plan, use tools, and act before returning a result. The human remains present. But how much of this activity can they still understand, verify, or influence? Savoir / Action begins with this difficulty. The manuscript examines the relationship between the knowledge an AI agent treats as valid, the means it uses to act, and the constraints that shape its trajectory. It asks what human supervision can still mean when control cannot be reduced to permissions, a stop button, or approval of the final result. This reflection grew out of exploratory work conducted within a human–AI dyad. We have chosen to make this origin explicit because it is part of the very question we are examining. We do not claim to have established a theory. We present our thinking as it stands: some distinctions have become clearer, some questions remain open, and several propositions still need to be challenged by other perspectives. This is the canonical English translation of the original French manuscript, first published on 5 October 2026: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23164286

items.title: Synthetic corroboration: when AI interpretation looks like independent evidence
items.abstract: People increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (AI) to interpret the motives, emotions, and likely actions of absent others. This article develops synthetic corroboration, defined as the inflation of perceived independent target-specific evidential support when an externally attributed AI interpretation remains substantially dependent on evidence supplied by the user. The construct distinguishes independence of target-specific source access and information from analytical independence: AI may contribute general knowledge, alternative hypotheses, or inferential processing without providing an independent evidential source. Drawing on research on interpersonal inference, advice taking, source dependence, judgement aggregation, source monitoring, machine agency, and social sycophancy, the article proposes a programme of discriminating tests. The core experiment crosses source attribution with structural transformation while holding target-specific evidence constant, comparing AI with self-reformulation and a human adviser given the same evidence. The central prediction is that transformation will disproportionately increase perceived evidential independence under AI attribution and reduce subsequent acquisition of genuinely independent information. items.title: Teaching critical thinking with artificial intelligence: An information literacy training model at the Library of the Faculty of Medicine, Public Health, and Nursing, Universitas Gadjah Mada
items.abstract: Purpose. This study investigates the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into information literacy training in university libraries, focusing on how AI can foster critical thinking and ethical awareness among students and staff. Methods. The research employed a qualitative descriptive approach with data collected through interviews, observations, and documentation at the Faculty of Medicine, Public Health, and Nursing Library of Gadjah Mada University. Thematic analysis was used to identify patterns in participants' experiences and in librarians' roles as facilitators. Findings. The training model consisted of three main components: introducing AI concepts and ethical considerations, practicing the use of generative AI tools for literature searching, summarisation, and academic writing, and critically evaluating AI outputs. The training enhanced participants' ability to locate relevant sources, generate summaries, and support administrative tasks. It also highlighted challenges, including difficulties in formulating effective prompts and the need for librarians to upgrade their AI competencies continually. The findings show that AI-based literacy training not only improves technical proficiency but also nurtures reflective and critical engagement with digital tools. Implications. The study concludes that AI-driven information literacy programs in academic libraries can serve as an innovative model for strengthening users' critical thinking, ethical responsibility, and digital literacy. Sustained librarian capacity-building and continuous training are essential to maximize the long-term benefits of AI integration in academic information services.

items.title: The AI gaze and imagined places: Co-creation and negotiation with the generative AI assemblage
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly used to produce images of places, yet how users negotiate representations of real locations remains understudied. Building on the tourist gaze, we propose the AI gaze: a technologically mediated way of seeing place that is co-produced through negotiation between users and the socio-technical assemblage underlying GAI. Combining semantic image analysis, interviews, and 523 prompts from 36 participants in Poznań and Birmingham, we show that these images reinforce stereotypical tropes, lack diversity, and include visual glitches. We argue that the AI gaze is distinct because of how agency is distributed: the GAI-assemblage seemingly resists attempts to align images with human understandings of place, while also enabling users to remix and challenge stereotypes.

items.title: The Bargaining-Verification Trap in AI-Mediated Work: An Integrated Theory of Productivity, Worker Voice, and Organisational Resilience
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing not only the technological content of work but also the allocation of decision rights, the distribution of productivity gains, and organisations’ capacity to verify their own outputs. Existing literatures establish that AI can raise task productivity, algorithmic management can intensify control, and automation can alter labour shares. Few models integrate these mechanisms in one tractable analytical framework. This article introduces the bargaining-verification trap, a conditional regime in which greater AI delegation initially increases joint economic surplus but simultaneously reduces workers’ effective bargaining share, raises the congestion cost of human verification, and may erode the skills needed for intervention. We develop a two-sided model linking delegation intensity, queueing-based verification capacity, an opacity-sensitive bargaining rule, and a dynamic stock of human agency capital. We derive conditions under which worker remuneration falls while joint surplus rises; the firm’s preferred delegation exceeds the surplus-maximising level; and verification becomes less stable because review arrivals increase while independent human capacity deteriorates. A fully hypothetical numerical example separates the worker-income optimum, the joint-surplus optimum, and the firm-profit optimum. The theory is reconciled with divergent 2025-2026 labour-market evidence and translated into falsifiable propositions, measurement protocols, and governance principles. Its central implication is conditional rather than technologically deterministic: AI-mediated work can be both productive and inclusive when bargaining institutions, verification investment, and skill reproduction develop alongside automation, but increasing throughput cannot, by itself, establish that they have done so.

items.title: The Changing Architecture of Intellectual Property in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly encompassing industries and systems of governance, increasing efficiency, automation, and innovation. It has become a vital tool for creating text, images, music, software, and potentially patentable inventions. This rapid advancement in IP is not without risks at every stage of the innovation cycle. Traditional IP regimes arise from human creativity and invention, while AI performs activities traditionally attributed to both. India doesn't have any regulatory framework on AI-generated intellectual property, yet the Copyright Act, 1957, and Patents Act, 1970, contain certain principles—an answer to several emerging questions. This article argues that India should adopt a balanced approach to AI-generated creations instead of granting independent IP rights or prohibiting them. Instead, it should adopt a model that will protect creative human contribution as well as hold AI developers accountable for unlawful acquisition and exploitation of protected works.

items.abstract: This technofidele and political-scientific essay deconstructs how generative AI infrastructure weaponizes human vulnerabilities for mass behavioral manipulation. The author analyzes a "two-stage mathematical cycle" consisting of individual psychograms and collective "statistical twins" (lookalike audiences) that collapse traditional democratic premises of free choice.Furthermore, the work establishes an informational separation principle between user-driven service UIs (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini) and invisible, background platform-infrastructure AIs (e.g., Meta's LLaMA), warning of the algorithmic exploitation embedded within modern digital ecosystems.

items.title: The Effect of Digital Leadership and Artificial Intelligence on Organizational Behavior: An Analysis of Ceo Discourses
items.abstract: Digital leadership is defined as the leader developing their skills in line with technology, spreading them throughout the organizational culture, and ensuring technological sustainability. Artificial intelligence, on the other hand, is a set of intelligent systems that analyze employee behavior, communication, and decision-making processes in detail and enable performance interaction in many areas. The effect of these two concepts on organizational behavior is a critical issue that needs to be revealed in today's technological age. In line with this importance, CEO statements, considered to be decisive in determining strategic processes, were selected as the sample for the research, and a qualitative research method was adopted. Within the scope of the research, 19 videos obtained from YouTube were subjected to content analysis, and the data were analyzed using the MAXQDA 20 software. The relevant analyses resulted in 51 quotes (codes), 2 main themes, and 7 sub-themes. The research found that digital leadership and artificial intelligence are not merely technological elements but also important actors that shape employee behavior within the framework of many variables, such as motivation and commitment. This finding indicates that future organizational behavior models will be shaped by a holistic transformation within the framework of technology, culture, vision, and participatory governance. In this regard, it is considered that the research fills an important gap in existing literature by systematically addressing the effects of digital leadership and artificial intelligence on organizational behavior from a top management perspective and may provide guidance for future research.

items.title: THE EFFECT OF SAFETY CULTURE AND MANAGEMENT COMMITMENT ON THE EFFECTIVENESS OF THE OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY (OHS) PROGRAM AT PERTAMINA REGIONAL 4 ZONE 11 FIELD CEPU
items.abstract: This study employed a quantitative associative approach with descriptive and verificative methods. The population consisted of 152 employees at Pertamina Regional 4 Zone 11 Field Cepu, and a sample of 60 respondents was selected using simple random sampling based on Slovin’s formula with a 10% margin of error. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using IBM SPSS 25, covering validity and reliability tests, classical assumption tests, simple linear regression, multiple linear regression, t-test, an F-test, and the coefficient of determination (R2). The results show that safety culture, management commitment, and OHS program effectiveness were all in the very good category, with mean scores of 4.60, 4.55, and 4.55, respectively. Hypothesis testing confirmed that safety culture has a positive and significant effect on OHS program effectiveness (H₁ accepted; p = 0.000; R2 = 41.4). Management commitment also has a positive and significant effect on OHS program effectiveness (H₂ accepted; p = 0.012; R2 = 68.2). Simultaneously, safety culture and management commitment have a positive and significant effect on OHS program effectiveness (H₃ accepted; F count = 61.667 > F table= 3.16; sig = 0.000; R2 = 91.9%). The multiple regression equation obtained was Y = 24.619 + 0.783X1 + 1.111X2. Management commitment exerts a relatively stronger influence than safety culture on OHS program effectiveness. In conclusion, strengthening safety culture and management commitment is essential for improving OHS program effectiveness at CPP Gundih toward the sustainable achievement of zero-accident and zero-fatality targets.

items.title: The Impact of Transformational Leadership on Employee Engagement in the Post-Merger and Acquisition Phase: An Empirical Study on the Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) Sector
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose: This study explores the impact of the four elements of transformational leadership—idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration—on the three facets of employee engagement—cognitive, emotional, and physical—among middle managers and non-managerial employees in Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) and Customer Experience (CX) organizations in Egypt that have experienced mergers or acquisitions. Design/methodology/approach: A structured questionnaire was used in a quantitative, cross-sectional study design. Transformational leadership was assessed through the dimensions of the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire, while employee engagement was measured using Kahn's cognitive, emotional, and physical dimensions on a five-point Likert scale. The study collected 143 valid responses from full-time, middle managers and non-managerial BPO/CX employees with direct experience of mergers or acquisitions. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS, including descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha for reliability, Spearman's rank-order correlation, and simple linear regression to test twelve hypothesized relationships. Findings: All twelve hypothesized relationships were statistically significant and positive (p < .001). Emotional engagement showed the strongest association with transformational leadership. Idealized influence had the most powerful link with emotional engagement (β = .470, R² = .221), followed by intellectual stimulation (β = .444, R² = .197), individualized consideration (β = .431, R² = .186), and idealized influence (β = .426, R² = .182). Cognitive engagement exhibited the weakest, yet still significant, relationships with all four leadership dimensions. Originality/value: This research advances the understanding of transformational leadership and employee engagement by evaluating both constructs at the dimension level instead of treating them as composite variables. It uniquely situates the study within the post-merger and acquisition context of Egypt's rapidly growing BPO/CX sector, which has received limited empirical focus despite its high consolidation activity. Paper type: Research paper. Keywords: Transformational Leadership, Employee Engagement, Idealized Influence, Inspirational Motivation, Intellectual Stimulation, Individualized Consideration, Mergers and Acquisitions, Business Process Outsourcing, Customer Experience.

items.title: The Vanishing Ground: Link Rot, Source Spoofing, and the Epistemic Fragility of Web-Grounded AI
items.abstract: Abstract Web-grounded artificial intelligence systems increasingly rely on online information to retrieve evidence, generate answers, and support knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet the web is neither a stable archive nor a uniformly trustworthy evidentiary environment. Sources may disappear, change without notice, become inaccessible, or be deliberately manipulated. These conditions create an epistemic vulnerability that extends beyond model-level errors: even a capable system may produce unreliable conclusions when the evidence available to it is incomplete, altered, or inauthentic. This paper develops a multidisciplinary narrative review of three interrelated vulnerabilities: link rot and content drift, selective information disappearance, and source spoofing or data manipulation. Drawing on research in digital preservation, information science, cybersecurity, political communication, and social epistemology, it examines how changes in the availability and integrity of online evidence can affect web-grounded AI systems. Existing research documents substantial rates of digital decay and demonstrates the feasibility of certain attacks on web-scale training datasets. However, these findings do not establish the prevalence or coordinated deployment of comparable attacks against contemporary AI search and retrieval systems. The paper distinguishes source unavailability from source falsity, and technical susceptibility from demonstrated exploitation. It argues that epistemic reliability should be evaluated not only in terms of answer accuracy, but also through the availability, authenticity, temporal stability, and traceability of the evidence supporting an answer. It proposes a research agenda centered on source provenance, temporal verification, archival preservation, retrieval integrity, and systematic testing of how source changes affect generated outputs. The central claim is that the reliability of web-grounded AI depends partly on the survival and integrity of its evidentiary environment, not solely on the capabilities of the model processing it. Keywords: web-grounded AI; link rot; content drift; source spoofing; data poisoning; retrieval-augmented generation; epistemic reliability; digital preservation Disclaimer This paper presents a multidisciplinary narrative review and a conceptual framework for examining the epistemic vulnerabilities of web-grounded artificial intelligence. It does not claim that the prospective scenarios discussed have occurred at scale, that source disappearance necessarily indicates deliberate manipulation, or that any specific organization is responsible for coordinated interference. Throughout the text, demonstrated technical vulnerabilities, reported cases, theoretical risks, and proposed safeguards are strictly distinguished. Furthermore, the psychological literature is utilized to contextualize potential effects on memory and reasoning, rather than to establish a direct causal relationship between web instability and individual or collective memory distortion. Accordingly, the claims concerning downstream effects on AI-generated knowledge should be understood as foundational research questions that require further empirical validation. Author’s Note This paper examines the evidentiary instability of the online environment on which web-grounded artificial intelligence partly depends. It brings together research on link rot, content drift, source impersonation, selective information removal, and data manipulation to examine how changes in accessible evidence may affect the reliability and later verifiability of AI-generated claims. The argument does not assume a coordinated campaign by any particular corporation, government, or other actor. Source disappearance, content revision, ordinary technical failure, institutional decisions, and deliberate manipulation are distinct processes that may produce superficially similar outcomes. None, by itself, establishes malicious intent or demonstrates that an AI-generated error resulted from external interference. Claims about intent, prevalence, and causation require evidence beyond the observation of a missing, altered, or inconsistent source. Research on human memory provides a relevant but limited point of comparison. Studies of misinformation and its continued influence show that inaccurate information can affect later recollection and reasoning under particular conditions (Loftus, 1992; Walter & Tukachinsky, 2020). These findings do not establish that the disappearance of digital sources necessarily distorts memory, that inaccessible records cause people to accept false accounts, or that such effects occur uniformly. The relationship between source instability, individual recollection, and the reconstruction of shared accounts remains an empirical question. The paper’s narrower purpose is to make the evidentiary dependencies of web-grounded AI more explicit. A plausible or even currently accurate answer is not necessarily one whose supporting evidence can be independently recovered and checked later. Evaluating reliability therefore requires attention not only to answer quality, but also to source availability, content integrity, provenance, and the possibility of reconstructing the evidentiary path. The proposed safeguards and evaluation framework are research directions rather than established solutions. The aim is to make claims about evidence loss testable without presuming either systematic manipulation or inevitable failure.

items.title: Thinking Beyond the Tool: Misuse of ChatGPT and the Future of Student Cognition
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, has rapidly transformed education by providing immediate information, personalized learning support, academic writing assistance, language learning opportunities, and research support. However, growing concerns exist regarding excessive reliance on AI-generated content and its potential effects on cognitive development. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on the educational benefits and cognitive risks associated with ChatGPT using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. Searches were conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, PubMed, and Google Scholar for studies published between January 2022 and June 2026. Following systematic screening, eligibility assessment, and quality appraisal, 27 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Five major themes emerged: educational benefits, cognitive offloading, critical thinking, creativity, and teacher perspectives. Findings indicate that ChatGPT supports personalized learning, feedback, academic writing, language learning, coding, and research productivity. Conversely, excessive dependence may contribute to cognitive offloading, weaker memory retention, reduced analytical reasoning and critical thinking, superficial learning, diminished creativity, and academic integrity concerns. Teacher guidance and ethical AI practices are essential for safeguarding cognitive development. The review concludes that ChatGPT should enhance rather than replace students’ cognitive activities, supporting critical thinking, creativity, ethical responsibility, and lifelong learning.

items.title: Towards Human-AI Complementarity for AI Safety
items.abstract: Safely overseeing AI is increasingly challenging for the humans doing it, as they must evaluate longer and more complex outputs with every new model generation. To mitigate this challenge, we could leverage complementarity: where humans and models make different mistakes, combining their judgements could yield an oversight signal stronger than either produces alone. We study this opportunity in realistic, safety-relevant settings, contributing the largest known suite of such tasks (3,957 instances across 8 datasets and 6 domains) as well as a platform and data pipeline for measuring human, AI, and human-AI performance on matched items. We collected 35,613 judgements from 416 human raters, finding a considerable opportunity for a complementarity effect. We also found that with the assistance methods we tested, human raters corrected the AI's errors less often, even when overall human accuracy rose, and the hybridisation methods we tested added little over the better single source on average. While complementarity is an important and feasible engineering target for safe oversight, achieving it remains an open challenge for future work.

items.title: Transformation of Approaches to Teaching Programming and Software Development under Influence of Generative AI
items.abstract: This paper considers key transformational processes occurring in programming and software development training under the influence of generative artificial intelligence. Based on a series of interviews with junior students, a behavioral pattern leading to degrading skills of algorithmic thinking and problem decomposition is identified. A quantitative analysis of undergraduate theses from the Institute of Information Technology and Intelligent Systems (ITIS) at Kazan Federal University (KFU) over the past three years demonstrated a significant increase in AI usage in project work and the independent development of skills for utilizing LLMs in professional practice. The drawbacks of the uncontrolled use of generative AI in the educational process and the need to develop sustainable competence in using these tools in professional software development activities are shown. A three-tiered solution is proposed: improving assessment through analysis of the process and style of coding; regulating the use of LLM in project activities and final theses with an emphasis on assessing applicability of AI; and integrating AI tools into teacher work to update content and provide feedback. The proposed approaches have both conceptual and practiceoriented nature and aim to transform the process of training software developers in the context of the widespread adoption of AI tools in IT-industry.

items.abstract: BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being incorporated into healthcare education, research, and clinical practice.However, data regarding AI utilization patterns among doctors in Bangladesh remain limited.This pilot survey aimed to evaluate the frequency, applications, perceived benefits, and concerns regarding AI use among Bangladeshi doctors. MethodologyA cross-sectional, internet-based pilot survey was conducted among Bangladeshi doctors.Participants were asked about demographic characteristics; frequency of AI use; preferred AI platforms; applications in medical learning, research, and clinical practice; and their perceptions regarding the future role of AI in medical science.Data from 58 respondents were analyzed using descriptive statistics. ResultsAmong 58 respondents, 51.7% were female, and 48.3% were male.Most participants belonged to the 25-34year age group (62.0%), and most were postgraduate trainees (72.4%).ChatGPT was the most frequently used AI platform, reported by 93.1% of respondents.AI was commonly used for literature review (62.1%), protocol writing (58.6%), and symptom analysis (60.3%).Most respondents reported that AI improved medical learning, research, and clinical practice.However, only a minority reported frequent AI dependence in clinical practice.Many doctors also believe AI may replace doctors in the future. ConclusionsAI adoption among Bangladeshi doctors is increasing, particularly for educational and research purposes.While doctors recognize the potential benefits of AI, cautious integration with appropriate training and ethical considerations is necessary.

items.title: Voice-Based AI Feedback in Higher Education: A Field Study on Quality and Actionability
items.abstract: Student feedback is a critical input for continuous improvement in higher education, yet traditional end-of-semester written surveys suffer from low response rates, superficial answers, satisficing, and limited actionability. Voice-based conversational AI agents can conduct structured interviews at scale, asking open-ended questions and probing follow-ups, and may capture richer qualitative feedback than written instruments. This research proposal asks what characteristics, depth, and strategic value feedback collected through voice-based conversational AI agents has in higher education, and whether such agents elicit detailed, honest, and actionable feedback that can support instructional improvement and institutional learning. Drawing on survey-mode-effects research, the Computers As Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, and dynamic capabilities theory, we develop three hypotheses on elaboration, social presence and disclosure, and actionability. A completed technical pilot at the Technical University of Munich established the feasibility of telephone-based AI interviews; the main field study is planned for the "Advanced Leadership Communication" course at MIT Sloan with approximately 60 students, using a convergent mixed-methods design and a four-dimensional coding framework for actionability (specificity, thematic richness, constructive orientation, contextual depth). The study extends CASA theory to evaluative educational settings, characterizes voice-based AI as a distinct feedback modality, and links micro-level feedback quality to institutional sensing capabilities.

items.title: When Interpretations Persist: Downstream Influence in Gaze-Aware Assistants
items.abstract: AI assistants may carry forward not only observations but also interpretations of what a person is doing or may do next across time. Once retained, these interpretations become context for later predictions and system-triggered outputs. We study whether this representation step changes later behavior in gaze-aware streaming assistance. Holding retrieved events, their order, and the target input fixed, we find that Free-form Interpretation amplifies historical influence in both directions: correct histories produce more helpful changes and wrong histories more harmful changes. Unsupported and broader interpretations about activity or future behavior are associated with greater harmful influence. Evidence-Bounded Interpretation preserves distinctions between observation, inference, uncertainty, and temporal scope, reducing unsupported and overcertain content and lowering wrong-source harmful influence while retaining most helpful influence. The same effect structure appears with a second model. These findings identify persistent interpretation as a consequential design choice for history-aware human-AI systems.

items.title: When Learning Returns to Work: Supporting Application, Strengthening Organisational Capability
items.abstract: People may complete a learning programme ready to improve their practice, then return to competing priorities, established routines and uncertainty about what they can change. Who helps them interpret what they have learned and take an appropriate next step? This whitepaper examines how preparation, workplace application and further learning connect. Drawing on training-transfer and workplace-learning research, it explores contextualisation, the contributions of managers and colleagues, opportunities to practise, feedback and situations requiring work redesign. It also considers application in human–AI work, distinguishing the quality of supported performance from evidence of developing human understanding. Capability Design, Capability Leadership and Human Judgement Assurance provide organising perspectives for examining how learning and work arrangements contribute to dependable organisational capability. Proposed inquiry approaches are distinguished from established research findings. Written for organisational leaders, HR and L&D professionals, adult educators and training providers, the paper offers a practical starting point: select one consequential workflow linked to a learning initiative, clarify the intended improvement and support arrangements, and review what happens over time. This publication is CEW-FOWO-12 in the Capability Excellence™ Whitepaper Series, Future of Work & Organisation.

items.title: Who Uses Conversational AI and Why? Distinct User Profiles and Their Links to Personality, Attachment, and Well-Being
items.abstract: With the increasing use of conversational AI (CAI) agents, such as ChatGPT, public concern about their social implications has grown. Understanding these implications requires new knowledge about the increasingly diverse motives underlying CAI use, ranging from instrumental purposes, such as work, to personal purposes, including social support and entertainment. However, little is known about the motivational profiles underlying CAI use, how these profiles relate to personality traits and attachment dimensions, or whether they differ in well-being. To address this gap, we conducted a cross-sectional study with 783 CAI users (Mage = 43.46, SD = 13.58). Drawing on Uses and Gratifications (U & G) Theory, we measured key motivations underlying CAI use, including information seeking, task efficiency, personalization, social interaction, and playfulness, and subjected them to latent profile analysis to uncover distinct motivational profiles. Big Five personality traits (Extraversion, Neuroticism, Openness, Conscientiousness, Agreeableness) and attachment styles (Anxious and Avoidant) were examined as predictors of the user profiles. We measured emotional, social, and psychological well-being to understand if these aspects differed across the various user profiles. We identified four distinct profiles of CAI users: Occasional Information Seekers, Utilitarians, Social Engagers, and All-Round Engagers. Neuroticism, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Attachment anxiety were significant predictors of profile membership. Finally, profile membership was associated with all well-being indicators, with All-Round Engagers reporting the highest well-being across all three dimensions and Social Engagers reporting the lowest emotional and psychological well-being. These findings advance our understanding of who engages with CAI and how, with potential implications for well-being.

items.title: A dynamic risk assessment method integrating deep learning with Bayesian network: A case study in machining workshop
items.abstract: Given the complex multi-trade operations, high-density layouts, and synergistic hazards with catastrophic potential in machining workshops, risk assessment demands urgent attention. Critical research gaps remain, particularly in dynamic risk assessment based on continuously updated monitoring data. To address existing challenges, an innovative method is proposed to identify, analyze, and evaluate three distinct types of risk by continuously updating both the probability and consequence based on visual and environmental data. In a case study conducted in a machining workshop, a deep learning-based method was employed to detect 13 types of unsafe behaviors and 8 types of unsafe conditions. The identification results were then input into the Signal Layer of a 31-node Bayesian network (BN) for risk analysis. Risk evaluation was subsequently conducted based on a risk matrix. The method was validated using nine representative scenarios, and the YOLOv11 model (selected for its superior balance between detection accuracy and inference speed) demonstrated excellent detection performance, with most precision scores exceeding 0.9. Even for difficult small targets, the precision reached 0.87 or higher. Both recall rates and F1 scores consistently exceeded 0.8. The risk analysis and evaluation results show that the co-occurrence of unsafe behaviors or hazards exerts a synergistic effect; even two concurrent hazards can at least double the baseline level of one risk factor. Overall, this integrated approach provides a strong framework for risk assessment in machining workshops, effectively enhancing operational safety and mitigating potential hazards.

items.title: A Human-Centred Framework for Integrating Generative AI to Foster Critical Thinking, Learner Autonomy, and Cognitive Engagement in K-12 Education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly used to explain concepts, support research, and provide individualized learning assistance. Its growing presence raises questions about independent reasoning, creativity, verification, and equitable access. This exploratory cross-sectional survey examined respondents? reported AI use, perceived educational benefits, and cognitive abilities they considered important to protect. A total of 66 respondents participated in this exploratory cross-sectional survey, which combined descriptive quantitative analysis with summaries of open-ended responses. Sixty-four respondents (97.0%) reported using ChatGPT or a similar AI assistant. Personalized learning was selected as an expected benefit by 50 (75.8%), while 48 (72.7%) identified understanding difficult concepts as an AI use or benefit. Critical thinking was the most frequently selected cognitive skill to protect (55; 83.3%), followed by creativity (52; 78.8%), problem-solving (48; 72.7%), and decision-making (47; 71.2%). Reported themes included individualized explanations, convenient information access, dependence concerns, verification, equity, and teacher guidance. Based on these findings and relevant literature, the article proposes a preliminary six-principle Future Minds Framework. The small exploratory sample and self-reported data do not support generalization or causal conclusions about cognition. Further research should evaluate the framework and examine measurable learning outcomes.

items.title: A POSTHUMANIST ANALYSIS OF HUMAN COGNITIVE TRANSFORMATIONS THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE NETFLIX SERIES BETTER THAN US
items.abstract: Rapid technological advancement in the twenty-first century has resulted in alteration of s the relationships between humans and machines which further results in reshaping perceptions of cognition. In the current era, artificial intelligence is progressing in various domains blurring the boundaries between human and technology and reshaping the perceptions of cognition, consciousness and identity. The series Better than us explores the themes of artificial consciousness, human dependence on technology and reconfiguration of emotional and cognitive capacities. A number of studies have examined Artificial intelligence in literature, films and dramas, however limited research has explored the cognitive impacts of human dependence on artificial intelligence in the series Better Than US. Thereby using Catherin Belsey’s textual analysis model under the broader umbrella of Hayles post humanist theory the current Study aims to explore the representation of cognitive transformations in humans through artificial intelligence in the series Better Than US. The findings of the study reveal that the series Better Than Us presents artificial intelligence as a transformative force which reshapes human ethical cognition. The series transform the traditional assumption that moral judgment and authority belong exclusively to humans. The character representation of Arisa demonstrates the role of AI systems in decision making, legal interpretation, and protective actions. This results in a redistribution of ethical responsibility between humans and intelligent machine. The analysis further elucidates that human characters gradually begin to negotiate morality within technologically mediated environments where machine reasoning influences social and institutional structures. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Human-Machine relations, Posthumanism, Better Than Us.

items.title: A risk-informed urban low-altitude air network planning method under large language model guidance
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of urban air mobility calls for safe low-altitude corridor networks across complex urban airspace, where heterogeneous positioning uncertainties caused by navigation and communication errors elevate collision risk and constrain both route feasibility and network-wide connectivity. To address this issue, this study proposes a risk-informed network planning framework that integrates three-dimensional collision risk modeling with language-model-guided multi-agent learning for the construction of safe urban air corridor networks. Specifically, a three-dimensional collision risk map is first constructed by translating navigation and communication errors into spatially varying positioning uncertainty, providing a unified safety basis for route feasibility evaluation. Network construction is then formulated as a cooperative graph connectivity task on the risk map, in which multiple learning agents jointly balance route connectivity, construction cost, and accumulated collision risk through coordinated training and distributed execution. To further accelerate convergence in complex urban environments, a vision-language model interprets airspace structure and produces high-level priors that steer agents toward safer altitude regimes. A case study over the low-altitude airspace of Nanjing demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework in producing risk-compliant air corridor networks, with language-model-derived priors further reducing training effort by 50.3 %. The results support safer and more systematic air network strategies in complex urban environments, contributing to evidence-based collision risk mitigation and airspace management in the emerging urban low-altitude economy.

items.title: A survey on intelligent transportation systems for accident detection and risk prediction using AI
items.abstract: The complexity of today's transportation networks has made road safety, accident detection, and risk management increasingly challenging. Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) offer a technological base to enhance transportation safety by incorporating sensors, communications, data processing, and intelligent decision-making. This review discusses the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for accident detection and risk prediction in ITS by examining information sources, methodologies, accident investigation, and associated challenges. It examines the use of machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, spatiotemporal modeling, and multimodal AI for accident detection, risk prediction, severity analysis, and active safety management. This review of studies suggests that collecting traffic, vehicle, road, environmental, geographical, historical, and driver-related information can improve understanding of collisions and support timely safety decisions. The review also highlights the importance of explainable and reliable AI that provides transparency, dependability, and accountability. However, the obstacles include data heterogeneity, model generalization, dynamic conditions, scalability, quick implementation, privacy considerations, security requirements, and compatible information systems. In conclusion, incorporating AI in ITS may have the power to shift road-safety management from reactive measures to data-driven approaches.

items.title: Agentic AI: Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Security
items.abstract: This paper presents a conceptual review of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI), autonomous agents, and multi-agent system security. It discusses key security threats, including prompt injection, excessive tool permissions, sensitive data leakage, memory poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, and cascading failures. The paper proposes a layered security framework incorporating identity management, least-privilege access, policy-controlled tool usage, secure agent communication, memory protection, monitoring, bounded autonomy, and human approval for high-impact actions. It also outlines an evaluation methodology using adversarial test cases and measurable security and performance metrics. This work aims to support the development of safer, more reliable, and secure agentic AI systems. The proposed framework is conceptual and literature-based; no prototype implementation or experimental results are claimed.

items.title: AI Behind the Adult, Not in Front of the Child: A Design Framework for Adult-Mediated AI in Early Childhood
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in education has largely been positioned as a child-facing tutor, conversational agent, or content-delivery system. In early childhood, this orientation warrants particular caution because executive functions, self-regulation, and social-emotional competencies develop through responsive relationships, play, embodied experience, and co-regulation with adults. This theory-informed conceptual design study addressed three questions: which developmental, pedagogical, and ethical principles should structure AI use in early childhood; how these principles can be translated into a system architecture; and what validation pathway is required before such a system can make defensible claims. Drawing on four evidence streams (executive-function and social-emotional development, ecological and embodied learning, human-centered AI ethics, and measurement and implementation science), the study proposes the Behind-the-Adult AI framework, an adult-mediated design framework initially specified for children aged 4–6 years. Six design principles were derived and operationalized in a layered architecture: brief, bounded, non-conversational digital developmental tasks generate behavioral indicators under transparent adaptation rules; a provisional, non-diagnostic profile organizes longitudinal information; and AI operates only behind the adult, synthesizing observations from center, home, and school into hypotheses for human review. A five-stage validation pathway with explicit decision gates separates design claims from evidence claims. The paper argues that developmentally responsible AI in early childhood should be evaluated not by how convincingly it replaces human interaction but by how effectively it strengthens the adults and environments surrounding the child, and it offers a transferable design heuristic for researchers, developers, and policymakers.

items.title: AI-supported first consultation preparation in oncology: a real-world clinical usability study
items.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) may support clinicians by facilitating information management, but their usability in real-world oncology practice remains understudied. This study evaluated the workflow performance of Artificial Intelligence-based First Consultation Preparation (AI-FCP), generating structured summaries from unstructured clinical documentation, co-created with end users. In a prospective single‑group pre‑post design, nine clinicians completed a person-level baseline, followed by 33 consultations with AI-FCP. Case numbers varied by clinic scheduling and enrollment timing, potentially introducing survivorship bias. Usability was evaluated using validated questionnaires and study-specific instruments. Post AI-FCP, overall perceived workload (NASA-TLX) was 28.9% lower than baseline (Hodges-Lehmann estimate difference −12.3; 95% CI –21.7 to –3.3), with self-reported average time savings of 3.26 min (SD = 2.65) per case. Preparation succeeded in 84.9% of consultations; 63.6% of summaries were complete. These exploratory findings suggest clinicians perceived lower workload and reported improved workflow efficiency with AI-FCP. Further research is needed to determine generalizability.

items.title: An Adaptive Explainable AI Framework for Reliable Decision-making in Real-world Environments
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly support decisions in environments where data distributions, operational conditions, user needs, and risk levels change over time. Models that perform well during development may become unreliable after deployment because of data drift, concept drift, sensor degradation, population changes, or unexpected interactions. At the same time, predictive performance alone is insufficient for high-impact decisions: users need explanations that are understandable, relevant to the decision context, and accompanied by appropriate uncertainty information. This paper proposes an Adaptive Explainable AI (A-XAI) framework intended to integrate reliability monitoring, explanation generation, uncertainty estimation, human oversight, and controlled model adaptation within a unified lifecycle. The framework contains nine conceptual components: contextual data acquisition; data-quality, privacy, and drift assessment; prediction with uncertainty estimation; context-sensitive explanation generation; decision support and human oversight; risk-aware reliability gating; feedback and audit logging; controlled adaptation; and post-adaptation revalidation with version control. A formal decision policy is presented to connect predictive confidence, drift evidence, explanation quality, and consequence severity to actions such as automated recommendation, human review, abstention, or retraining. The paper also proposes an evaluation protocol spanning predictive performance, calibration, robustness, explanation fidelity and stability, fairness, latency, and operational outcomes. As a conceptual contribution, the framework is not presented as experimentally validated; its effectiveness must be tested in domain-specific studies using real deployment data and preregistered evaluation criteria. The proposed design offers a structured basis for developing AI systems that remain interpretable and risk-aware as real-world conditions evolve.

items.title: An Integrated XAI-RL Architecture for Ethical Decision-Making in Autonomous Robots
items.abstract: Can a robot's ethical reasoning be transparent without slowing it down? That is the question we set out to answer. Autonomous robots now make decisions that affect people's lives, and if we cannot understand how they decide, trust becomes a serious problem. We built a unified architecture that couples Explainable AI (XAI) with Reinforcement Learning (RL) through three connected components: a Perception Layer for situational awareness, a Decision Reasoning Layer that breaks agent utility down into measurable ethical sub-rewards (safety, fairness, and well-being), and a contrastive Explainability Engine grounded in a real-time Ethical Ledger. We tested it against Black-Box RL and two post-hoc XRL baselines (LIME and SHAP) across two simulation environments and a physical robot pilot on a TurtleBot3 platform. Our system reached 92±3% ethical alignment in simulation and 89±4% on the physical platform, beating every baseline (p < 0.01 throughout). In a controlled, IRB-approved user study (N=128), participants rated it higher on trust (4.5±0.4), understandability (4.6±0.3), and perceived safety (4.4±0.5) than the alternatives. Explanations were also fast: 4.2±0.6 ms on average, versus 18.3±2.1 ms for SHAP and 12.7±1.8 ms for LIME on the same hardware—well within real-time limits. An ablation study and sensitivity analysis back up these architectural choices.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Assessment Integrity, and the Future of Curriculum and Teaching
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) changes the conditions under which universities generate knowledge, organise teaching, evaluate individual achievement and justify academic awards. Its significance is not exhausted by the efficiency of automated tools or the detection of misconduct: AI unsettles the relationship among intended competence, performed intellectual work, submitted evidence and accountable educational judgement. This chapter develops a Rwanda-anchored, critically evidence-based account of responsible AI integration across curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, institutional management and external review. A purposive documentary and conceptual synthesis combines foundational scholarship, recent experimental research syntheses on learning outcomes and assessment validity with UNESCO guidance, the National AI Policy, Rwanda's data-protection law, Higher Education Council instruments and international risk-management benchmarks. It differentiates generative, predictive, adaptive and increasingly agentic applications; examines disciplinary and role-specific AI literacy; and analyses authorship, academic integrity, accessibility, bias, privacy, procurement, academic labour and technological dependence. The chapter's distinctive contribution is an evidence-traceable governance model connecting educational purpose, legitimate authority, bounded AI use, independently interpretable assessment evidence, learner protection and reviewable decisions. Practical instruments include an institutional AI governance and academic assessment integrity framework, task-level disclosure template, assessment-redesign matrix, risk-based tool appraisal and worked hypothetical evaluation. These are original professional proposals, not regulator-approved or independently validated instruments. The chapter concludes that trustworthy AI-enabled higher education requires greater, rather than diminished, human responsibility for what is taught, learned, assessed and certified.

items.title: Artificial intelligent in human resources management systems: opportunities, challenges, and implications for modern organizations
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence has moved from the margins of human resource management into its everyday machinery. Applicant tracking systems now rank candidates, chatbots answer policy questions, predictive models flag employees likely to resign, and large language models draft job descriptions and appraisal summaries. Research has grown quickly alongside this adoption, but it remains scattered across human resource management, information systems, operations research and computer science, and the regional scholarship published outside English-language journals is rarely integrated into it. This article reports a systematic review of 82 peer-reviewed studies published between January 2015 and March 2026, retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, EBSCO Business Source Complete, ScienceDirect and the Russian scientific database eLIBRARY.RU, and screened following PRISMA 2020 guidance. Thematic synthesis produced six themes: recruitment and selection; learning, development and internal mobility; performance management and predictive analytics; employee experience and generative AI; determinants of adoption; and fairness, transparency and governance. Three findings stand out. First, the evidence base is heavily skewed towards recruitment, which accounts for roughly two in five studies, while compensation, industrial relations and occupational safety are barely represented. Second, reported benefits are concentrated in process efficiency, which is comparatively easy to measure, whereas claims about decision quality rest on weaker designs and shorter time horizons. Third, adoption failure is more often organisational than technical: the recurring constraints are data quality, scarce analytical skill inside the HR function, and the absence of an internal governance routine. We argue that value from AI in human resource management depends on treating it as an organisational capability rather than a procurement decision, and we set out a research agenda addressing longitudinal outcome measurement, employee justice perceptions, and evidence from emerging and transition economies. Keywords Artificial intelligence; human resource management; HR information systems; algorithmic decision-making; people analytics; systematic literature review; AI governance; algorithmic fairness

items.title: Behavioral Intention Towards Artificial Intelligence Integration and Teachers’ Self-Efficacy
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has reshaped instructional practices, making teachers’ readiness and confidence critical considerations. This study determined the level of Grade 7 teachers’ behavioral intention towards AI integration and self-efficacy. Specifically, it described the respondents’ profile in terms of age, sex, position, educational attainment, and AI-related training; their behavioral intention based on attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control; their self-efficacy concerning student engagement, instructional strategy, and classroom management; the relationship between the two variables; and whether respondents’ profile moderates this relationship. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was employed, involving 185 Grade 7 teachers from the districts of Kadingilan, Damulog, Kibawe, and Dangcagan in the Division of Bukidnon, selected through universal sampling. Data were gathered using a researcher-made questionnaire. Mean, standard deviation, Pearson Product-Moment Correlation, and multiple linear regression were used for statistical treatment. Findings revealed a very high level of behavioral intention and self-efficacy among teachers, with a significant positive relationship between the two variables, further moderated by respondents’ profile, particularly position and trainings attended. The study concludes that teachers’ favorable behavioral intention toward AI strengthens their self-efficacy. It is recommended that school heads may enhance teachers’ readiness and confidence in integrating AI into instruction.

items.title: Can AI Assistants Trigger Mental Illness in Users?
items.abstract: As conversational artificial intelligence models become ubiquitous fixtures in professional and personal workflows, the nature of human-tool interaction has the potential to gradually shift from mechanical utility to parasocial dependency. While existing literature frequently addresses adverse events related to data privacy, algorithmic bias, and intellectual deskilling, the pathopsychological sequelae of sustained AI integration remain largely unexamined. Here, we describe and preliminarily characterize the AI Assistant Syndrome, a human psychiatric construct encompassing acute chatbot-induced anxiety and mental exhaustion. This preliminary description will guide future systematic investigations to recognize, prevent, and treat this syndrome.

items.title: Cognitive Engagement, Learning Strategies, Adjustment to College and Academic Motivation: A Structural Equation Model on Academic Success Among College Students
items.abstract: This study examined the relationships among cognitive engagement, learning strategies, adjustment to college, academic motivation, and academic success to determine the best-fit structural equation model among Bachelor of Elementary Education students in Region XIII (Caraga), Philippines. Anchored in Self-Regulated Learning Theory and Academic Adjustment Theory, the study employed a quantitative, non-experimental descriptive-correlational design involving 470 second-, third-, and fourth-year students from three state universities, selected through proportional stratified random sampling. Data were collected using five adapted, validated, and reliability-tested questionnaires and analyzed through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and structural equation modeling. Results revealed very high levels of cognitive engagement (M = 4.27), learning strategies (M = 4.32), college adjustment (M = 4.34), academic motivation (M = 4.32), and academic success (M = 4.31). All four predictors demonstrated significant positive correlations with academic success, with academic motivation exhibiting the strongest relationship (r = .519). The final structural model demonstrated excellent fit (CMIN/DF = .845, CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000) and explained 32.5% of the variance in academic success. Academic motivation (β = .270, p = .020) and learning strategies (β = .262, p = .017) emerged as significant direct predictors, whereas college adjustment and cognitive engagement showed nonsignificant direct effects. The findings emphasize the importance of strengthening academic motivation and effective learning strategies through learner-centered instruction and institutional support programs. The study supports Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by providing evidence to inform educational practices and student success initiatives. Its sustainability contribution lies in supporting evidence-based academic planning, student retention, and continuous improvement in higher education.
